C.5 ISO New England’s Greater Boston Transmission Project The Greater Boston Transmission Project is a reliability project consisting of a portfolio of new transmission lines, reconductoring of existing lines, new transformers, and other transmission- related upgrades. It illustrates the ISO’s approach to planning transmission projects around project costs rather than project benefits. Costs for regional reliability projects are allocated on a postage stamp basis to the region using load ratio share. Reliability projects must satisfy evaluation factors defined in Attachment K and reliability standards in Attachment N of the ISO’s tariff (ISO-NE 2025a). The tariff defines the criteria that ISO-NE may use in selecting proposals to satisfy reliability needs, but there is no benefit quantification for reliability projects. The ISO’s Transmission Cost Allocation Review process can be summarized in four steps (ISO-NE 2023a): 1. Transmission owners submit a transmission cost allocation application, requesting regional rate recovery for their project(s). 2. ISO reviews project costs and determines if costs are “reasonable and in accordance with good utility practice.” 3. The Reliability Committee provides advisory input to ISO-NE on whether the proposed project includes localized costs. 61 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4. ISO determination of how much of project’s costs are applicable for regional cost recovery. The Greater Boston Transmission Project was one of the largest and most expensive reliability projects planned in the ISO-NE, originally estimated to be $822 million (ISO-NE 2023b). The Reliability Committee voted to recommend the project in June 2017. Costs for reliability projects are generally based on load ratio share. The final cost allocation for this project has not been determined yet. In September 2020, an additional $188.6 million was requested to underground a 115-kV transmission line originally designed as an overhead line but was unable to secure property rights. The Reliability Committee did not recommend approval of this request, and the additional cost for the undergrounding project remains under review by ISO-NE (ISO-NE 2020). C.6 MISO-SPP Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue Projects The JTIQ concept originated from developers that wanted to build and interconnect generation along the MISO-SPP seam but were facing prohibitive interconnection costs. A joint study by MISO and SPP originally identified seven projects with a total cost of roughly $1.6 billion (MISO 2022). Two of the initial 7 JTIQ projects were found to have benefits to load and qualify as MVP projects in MISO’s tariff and were removed from JTIQ and placed in MISO’s Long Range Transmission Planning Tranche 1 portfolio (SPP and MISO 2022a). The initial JTIQ study (SPP and MISO 2022b) established a cost allocation methodology for JTIQ projects similar to MISO’s generator interconnection cost allocation scheme, whereby 90% of the engineering and construction costs are paid for by the interconnecting generators and 10% is paid for by load in SPP and MISO in proportion to each region’s calculated adjusted production cost benefit.
